As of 308 AM Sunday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... Scattered to locally numerous showers/storms late 
this morning into the early evening hours will be capable of brief, 
short-track tornadoes and strong to severe wind gusts.

The remnants of Isaias are presently across eastern TN. With time, 
this area of low pressure will track into the Mid-Atlantic this 
evening and eventually off New England overnight tonight. A 
secondary area of low pressure is forecast to develop near Charlotte 
this morning, tracking into the NW Piedmont this afternoon before 
reaching central VA this evening. As this does so, a warm front 
presently across SC will lift north this morning, ahead of a strong 
cold front that will sweep through this afternoon and early evening.

Overall, there has been minimal change to the going forecast through 
tonight. The main uncertainty lies in overall coverage of scattered 
showers and storms. SPC has maintained a Level 2 Slight Risk for 
eastern areas of central NC, from the Triangle/Sandhills eastward 
and a Level 1 Marginal Risk across the western and southern 
Piedmont. The latest HREF/REFS solutions are indicating a more 
focused tornado threat across the far northeast Piedmont into VA, 
closer to the triple point and area of low pressure. However, in 
this environment with strong deep-layer shear and clockwise turning, 
a brief tornado threat will exist nearly anywhere in central NC.

The greatest severe risk is favored from 11 AM to 6 PM today, based 
on a suite of ensemble/model guidance and the timing of the cold 
front/dry slot. Ahead of the front, a moisture-rich environment will 
exist with low/mid 70s dewpoints, supporting 1000-1500 J/kg of 
MLCAPE. This axis of instability and shear overlaps most favorably 
from the Triangle/Sandhills into the central/northern Coastal Plain. 
CAM solutions indicate a broken band of showers and storms moving 
east-northeast in this time frame. Although an isolated tornado 
could happen anywhere, the greatest risk for short-track tornadoes 
appears to be from the Triangle to the north and east, roughly from 
Raleigh to Goldsboro to Rocky Mount/Henderson and northeast into 
Roanoke Rapids. In this region, forecast soundings indicate long 
curved hodographs supportive of discrete supercells. Outside of the 
tornado risk, strong to severe wind gusts will be possible across 
all of central NC. The severe threat should greatly diminish after 6 
PM as activity races NE into the Mid-Atlantic coast.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Much of next week will be unseasonably warm, before 
a significant cooldown next weekend. Little if any precipitation is 
expected through the period.

Broad mid/upper ridging over the Southeastern US (in between 
troughing over the North Atlantic that will absorb the remnants of 
Isaias and a closed low over the Intermountain West) will bring 
mostly sunny and dry weather to central NC for much of the upcoming 
workweek. At the surface, a low will track east from the Great Lakes 
into northern New England from Tuesday into early Wednesday, 
dropping a backdoor cold front southward into the Mid-Atlantic. 
Southerly flow ahead of the front will bring increasing temperatures 
to start the week, with highs in the upper-70s to lower-80s on 
Monday and lower-to-mid-80s on Tuesday. Due to a slower trend with 
the low's translation eastward, the front now doesn't look like it 
will cross central NC until Wednesday night or Thursday. This 
results in a much warmer forecast for Wednesday and potential record 
or near record highs, which are now expected to be in the mid-to-
upper-80s, and lows in the lower-to-mid-60s. Thursday's temperatures 
will depend on the exact timing of the front, but they should turn 
at least a bit more seasonable, albeit still warmer than normal. The 
front will be moisture-starved and devoid of any upper support for 
precipitation with the ridge in place, so it should be mainly dry 
with just some associated cloud cover.

A more vigorous northern stream shortwave will then dive down from 
Canada in the northern Plains and Great Lakes region late in the 
week and potentially interact with the Western US trough, which 
should help suppress the Southeast US ridge over the weekend. 
Guidance is in better agreement that the low will help lift the 
aforementioned boundary back north as a warm front on Friday, but 
significant differences in the pattern still exist, with the GFS 
continuing to show a phasing solution that results in a much 
deeper/slower trough (and associated surface low) compared to the 
ECMWF. The low will drag a much stronger cold front through central 
NC, but the exact timing is still uncertain, sometime on Friday or 
Saturday. Regardless the best forcing looks to be well to our north 
so any associated precipitation would be light, and POPs are only 
slight chance at best. A significant cooldown to below-normal
